title: Do Canonical Network Verifiers Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM→Config Pipelines?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study that tests whether interposing a deterministic network verifier (generate→verify pipeline) reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated network configurations that would execute with operational faults in an isolated emulation environment. Using a shared_initial_candidate paired design, one initial LLM candidate per intent (gpt-5-mini) was executed either directly (baseline) or after deterministic verification (guarded). We evaluated 72 preregistered intent pairs (144 episodes total) on synthetic but policy‑constrained topology tasks. Primary result: both baseline and guarded conditions produced valid, non‑faulting configurations for all 72 pairs (n_11 = 72), giving a paired difference estimate 0.0 (95% bootstrap CI 0.0–0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). Confirmatory conclusion: under the chosen model, task set, and shared_initial_candidate semantics, the verifier did not reduce any undetected faults because no undetected faults occurred in the baseline executions (ceiling effect). Exploratory diagnostics show no verifier false negatives to categorize. We report the preregistered design, deterministic execution manifest, exact analysis outcomes, and limitations; we discuss how task realism, adversarial stress tests, multi‑model sampling, and independent‑generation designs are required to evaluate practical verifier utility.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are being proposed as intent→configuration translators for network operations (NetOps). Prior work shows promising task‑level translation accuracy but highlights operational risk from semantic errors, ordering mistakes, and protocol violations that can cause incorrect or unsafe network changes [1], [2]. A common mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture that interposes deterministic validators before execution [3]. This study asks the preregistered question: does coupling an LLM generator with a canonical deterministic network verifier materially reduce the fraction of LLM candidates that would execute with operational faults, compared with executing the same LLM candidate without verifier intervention? Our confirmatory contribution is an evidence‑grounded paired experiment (shared_initial_candidate) with an archival execution manifest, deterministic analysis, and exact inferential accounting.
sections.related_work: Intent→configuration transformation using LLMs has been demonstrated in controlled studies and prototypes that combine fine‑tuning and in‑context learning for common vendor dialects and use cases [1]. Multi‑agent and tool‑augmented frameworks integrate validation tooling to reduce regressions in production settings [2], but public evidence is limited. The generate–verify–repair pattern has been proposed and instantiated in code and software repair domains to reconcile stochastic generation with deterministic verification oracles [3]. Network verification tools such as header‑space/NetPlumber enable fast static checks of forwarding and policy invariants and are natural candidates for the verifier role in NetOps GVR stacks [4]. Prior surveys and architectural proposals motivate GVR in NetOps but do not supply systematic paired experiments using shared initial candidates and preregistered estimands.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: we preregistered study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001. The primary estimand is the paired reduction in the proportion of undetected operational faults (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The execution contract used shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single initial LLM generation was produced per intent and that exact candidate was evaluated under both conditions. Model and interface: all initial generations used gpt-5-mini (declared model_version in the manifest). Task bank and scope: 72 confirmatory intent pairs were sampled from a synthetic, provenance‑recorded task corpus stratified across three topology complexity strata (preregistration details archived). Adapter and environment: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 served as the verifier; emulated end‑to‑end execution was performed in isolated images per the preregistered emulator plan. Call budget and retries: one initial generation per intent (shared) with up to preregistered retries for transient provider errors; total model calls used = 72. Analysis plan: exact paired binary inference (McNemar‑style exact test), bootstrap CIs for descriptive rates, and pre‑specified sensitivity analyses (e.g., conservative treatments for excluded pairs). All design choices, seeds, exclusion rules, and stopping rules were preregistered and are included in the archived preregistration.
sections.results: Execution and manifest: the registered run completed (execution_manifest). Completed_episode_count = 144 (72 paired intents); model_calls_used = 72. Confirmatory outcome: for every paired intent the same initial candidate produced a valid, non‑faulting execution in the emulator under both baseline and guarded conditions. Contingency counts: n_11 = 72, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed reported in artifacts) = [0.0, 0.0]. Secondary estimands: no verifier true positives or false negatives were observed because no emulator failures occurred in baseline. Missingness and exclusions: none; all preregistered pairs completed. All raw outputs, validator traces, and reconciliations are archived and referenced in the execution manifest.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: the confirmatory hypothesis H1 (that the guarded pipeline reduces undetected faults relative to baseline) is not supported in this run because both conditions produced zero undetected faults. This outcome is a valid scientific observation: under the chosen model (gpt-5-mini), prompt/task corpus, and shared_initial_candidate semantics, the generator produced configurations that passed both deterministic validation and emulator execution for every item. Methodological implication: a paired, shared_initial_candidate test cleanly measures verifier benefit only when baseline candidates include faults the verifier can detect; a ceiling effect (zero baseline faults) prevents the experiment from evaluating the verifier's detection power. Relation to prior work: our result does not contradict prior claims that GVR can reduce defects [3]; rather, it shows that verifier utility depends on generator error rates and task realism. Limitations (confirmatory vs exploratory): the confirmatory outcome is exact for the executed contract but exploratory questions (which fault categories the verifier misses, topology sensitivity under adversarial prompts, multi‑model variance) remain unanswered. Practical implications: when generator quality is high on constrained synthetic tasks, a verifier may offer little marginal benefit for single‑shot candidates; however, this does not generalize to adversarial or broader production tasks without further evaluation. Future work: evaluate (a) adversarial/fault‑injection tasks, (b) independent per‑condition generations to test prompt sensitivity and sampling variability, (c) additional models and verifier combinations, and (d) larger, less curated topology/policy corpora to avoid ceiling effects.
sections.conclusion: We ran a preregistered, paired evaluation under shared_initial_candidate semantics to test whether a deterministic network verifier reduces undetected operational faults in LLM→configuration pipelines. For the 72 preregistered intent pairs and the chosen model and verifier, baseline generations produced zero emulator faults and the verifier therefore did not change the outcome (paired difference 0.0, p = 1.0). This null confirmatory result illustrates that (i) verification benefit depends on the generator error profile and task realism and (ii) rigorous evaluation of GVR in NetOps requires adversarial, diverse, and production‑representative tasks or designs that induce generator errors the verifier can detect. We release the execution manifest, raw outputs, and analysis artifacts to support follow‑on studies and community benchmarks.

limitations: Confirmatory result is a null/ceiling outcome: the baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit.

Shared_initial_candidate design (preregistered) measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only; it does not assess independent generation strategies or alternative prompting that produce different candidates.
Single‑model scope: experiments used a single declared model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across models or model releases.
Synthetic, provenance‑recorded tasks and emulator execution differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to diverse production deployments is limited.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance checks were applied and public‑corpus exact matches excluded per preregistration, but private training‑data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and is acknowledged as residual uncertainty.
